newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore economy grows surprise seven pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Singapore economy grows surprise seven pct in 1996.

text.p: Singapore's economy grew by seven percent in 1996, above the previous official estimate of 6.5 percent, Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said on Friday.
Lee told a meeting of local business leaders that the country should comfortably achieve its official forecast economic expansion of five to seven percent in 1997.
The economy grew by 8.8 percent in 1995 and 10.2 percent in 1994, official figures show.
Economists were surprised by the 1996 growth figure, saying it meant the economy was back on track for a strong expansion in 1997.
Lee said the economy slowed last year due to a slump in the global electronics industry, which accounts for around half of Singapore's industrial output and almost 60 percent of its non-oil exports.

"After three to four boom years, the global electronic industry took some correction to allow the industry to shed its excessive inventory. Slower growth in regional countries also affected our hub services like shipping and entrepot trade," Lee told the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
But he said the slowdown had been "a welcome breather", which had allowed the economy to consolidate.

"Already, the Singapore economy has shown signs of recovery. After a weak 3.3 percent in 3Q 1996, economic growth in 4Q 1996 rebounded to 5.8 percent, better than we expected. This brings full year growth in 1996 to 7.0 percent," he said.
These figures are all higher than previous official data.

Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said in December the economy grew by 6.5 percent, in line with a recent Reuters' poll of economists. The government had previously said growth was 3.2 percent in the third quarter and 4.0 percent in the fourth.
Lee said the prospects for the Singapore economy this year were good.
"MTI (the Ministry of Trade and Industry) has earlier predicted steady growth of between five to seven percent. Judging from recent trends, we should be able to achieve this comfortably," he said.
He said a pick-up in global demand for electronics would flow through to Singapore "in due course".
"In recent months, U.S. new orders for electronics components have also increased, while inventory levels continued to decline," he said.
Desmond Supple, emerging markets analyst at I.D.E.A. in Singapore, said the higher than expected growth in 1996 heralded a healthy recovery in economic activity this year.
"This is a pleasant surprise," Supple said. "Singapore appears to have handled the electronics slowdown very well."
"The economy is set to rebound above forecast growth this year. We had forecast 7.5 percent and may now have to revise that upwards," he said.
